title: PEM, DER and PFX
summary: Tell certificate files apart by what is inside, not by their extension.

steps.title: Same certificate, different wrappers
body: A certificate is a structure encoded in **DER**: compact binary bytes. Everything else is packaging.
| Format | What it is | Looks like | Usual extensions |
| **DER** | the raw binary bytes | starts with byte `0x30` | `.cer`, `.der`, `.crt` |
| **PEM** | DER in Base64 between header lines | `-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----` | `.pem`, `.crt`, `.cer` |
| **PEM key** | a private key in Base64 | `-----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----` | `.key`, `.pem` |
| **PFX / PKCS#12** | a password-protected bundle: certificate(s) **plus** private key | binary | `.pfx`, `.p12` |
The key lesson: **the extension does not tell you the format**. A `.cer` can be DER or PEM; a `.crt` can be either.
Open it in a text editor: readable `-----BEGIN` lines mean PEM, gibberish means DER or PFX.
A PEM file can hold several blocks one after another. A `fullchain.pem` is the leaf, then its intermediate(s).

steps.prompt: Does this file give you a private key?
steps.explain: Certificate blocks are public no matter how many there are. A PFX/P12 is the usual way to carry a certificate together with its key.

steps.prompt: You open `server.cer` in Notepad and see `-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----` followed by lines of letters. A tool insists the file is "not valid DER". What is going on?
options: The file is PEM; convert it to DER or tell the tool to read PEM
The file needs its private key added
`.cer` files are always DER, so the issuer made a mistake
steps.explain: The `.cer` extension is used for both. `openssl x509 -in server.cer -outform der -out server.der` converts, and many tools have an `-inform pem` style switch.

steps.prompt: `ExportCertificatePem()` wraps the DER bytes in PEM. What does this print?
code: using var cert = new CertificateRequest("CN=demo", key, HashAlgorithmName.SHA256).CreateSelfSigned(
steps.explain: DER always begins with `0x30` (an ASN.1 SEQUENCE). Base64 of `30 82 ...` starts with `MII`, which is why almost every PEM certificate body begins with those letters.

steps.title: Converting between formats
body: You will meet these commands constantly. Read them, recognise them:
```text
openssl x509 -in cert.der -inform der -out cert.pem                  DER -> PEM
openssl x509 -in cert.pem -outform der -out cert.der                 PEM -> DER
openssl pkcs12 -export -in cert.pem -inkey cert.key -out site.pfx    PEM cert + key -> PFX
openssl pkcs12 -in site.pfx -nokeys -out cert.pem                    PFX -> certificate only
certutil -dump site.pfx                                              inspect on Windows
In .NET:
```csharp
var cert = X509Certificate2.CreateFromPem(certPem, keyPem);     // .crt + .key -> cert with key
byte[] pfx = cert.Export(X509ContentType.Pfx, "pw");            // -> PFX bytes
var back = X509CertificateLoader.LoadPkcs12(pfx, "pw");         // PFX -> cert with key
string pem = cert.ExportCertificatePem();                       // public cert as PEM

steps.prompt: Kestrel needs a certificate **with** its private key. Your CA emailed `shop.crt`, and you generated `shop.key` yourself when you made the request. What do you do?
options: Load both: `X509Certificate2.CreateFromPem(crt, key)`, or combine them into a PFX with `openssl pkcs12 -export`
Ask the CA to send the private key
Use `shop.crt` alone; the key is inside it
Generate a new key and use it with `shop.crt`
steps.explain: The CA never sees your private key: you sent it a *certificate signing request* containing only the public key. The certificate only works with the key that matches the public key inside it, so a new key is useless with this certificate.

steps.title: PEM by hand
prompt: PEM is simple enough to write yourself. Write `string ToPem(byte[] der)` that returns:
<Base64 of der, broken into lines of 64 characters>
Join lines with `\n` and add no trailing newline. The last Base64 line may be shorter than 64.
**Run checks** compares your output with .NET's own `ExportCertificatePem()`.
starter: // split b64 into 64-character lines and add the header and footer
hints: Loop `for (int i = 0; i < b64.Length; i += 64)` and take `Math.Min(64, b64.Length - i)` characters.
Put the header first and the footer last, then `string.Join("\n", lines)`.
template: Dojo.Eq("Short input fits on one line", "-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----\nAQID\n-----END CERTIFICATE-----", ToPem(new byte[] { 1, 2, 3 }));
Dojo.Eq("Exactly 48 bytes (64 Base64 chars) makes one full line", 3, ToPem(new byte[48]).Split('\n').Length);
static X509Certificate2 DojoCert(string subject, X509Certificate2? issuer, bool isCa, string? dns = null, string? eku = null, int nbYear = 2030, int naYear = 2035)
var req = new CertificateRequest(subject, key, HashAlgorithmName.SHA256);
req.CertificateExtensions.Add(new X509KeyUsageExtension(isCa ? X509KeyUsageFlags.KeyCertSign | X509KeyUsageFlags.CrlSign : X509KeyUsageFlags.DigitalSignature, true));
if (dns != null) { var b = new SubjectAlternativeNameBuilder(); foreach (var d in dns.Split(',')) b.AddDnsName(d); req.CertificateExtensions.Add(b.Build()); }
if (eku != null) req.CertificateExtensions.Add(new X509EnhancedKeyUsageExtension(new OidCollection { new Oid(eku) }, false));
using var pub = req.Create(issuer, nb, na, serial);
